tone_statements.citation: Niederer, Barbara. 2002. Introduction to Chángpáoyáo. Cahiers de Linguistique Asie Orientale 31(2): 211-243. Paris: CRLAO-EHESS. doi:10.3406/clao.2002.1611 (also Brill doi:10.1163/19606028-90000105).
tone_statements.quote: Unstopped monosyllables {i.e. open syllables and syllables closed with /-n, -n, -ml can have one of nine contrasing tones; monosyllables ending in /-p, -t, -k/ can take either of two tones. Although the tones of stopped and unstopped syllables are a bit different phonetically, the tones of the syllables stopped by /-p, -t, -k/ can be identified with tones 7 and 8 of unstopped syllables. 1.55 2.35 3.33 4.11 5.52 6.42 7.45(4) 8.2(3)2 З'.ПЗ Numbering of tones follows historical categories. ... No tone sandhi has been discovered so far.
tone_statements.locator: pp.222-224, §2.3 'Tones' (tone-value line and 'Numbering..' on p.223; 'No tone sandhi..' on p.224)
tone_statements.summary: Dongmeng/Changpaoyao (Dongtang): 9 tones on smooth syllables 55 35 33 11 52 42 45(4) 2(3)2 + 3'=113; checked syllables only T7 45 / T8 11; breathy T6,T8; no tone sandhi; toneless (neutral) presyllables.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page numa1251 'Numao' (alt. name Nu-hmou); refs Meng 2001:149-192, Niederer 2002:216, Ratliff 2010.
sources.note: Bibliographic/classificatory only; zero descriptive references attached to numa1251 itself.

Nothing on stress; give autonyms nu22 m̥ou11 (Numao, ~1,200 speakers, Yaolu and Jiarong townships) and toŋ11 m̥uŋ11 (Dongmeng, ~400 speakers, Maolan/Dongtang/Weng'ang), 1,715 speakers (2001), citing Meng 2001, Zhou Guoyan 2013 and Guizhou sheng zhi: Minzu zhi 2002.

sources.citation: Ratliff, Martha. 2010. Hmong-Mien Language History. Pacific Linguistics 613. Canberra: The Australian National University. (Open Access, CC BY-SA, hdl 1885/146760)
sources.note: No Numao/Yaolu data at all (its Bunu data points are Qibainong Bunu = Dongnu and 'Yaoli Bunu' = Nao Klao of Nandan, Wang & Mao 1995 #10/#11, plus Meizhu Bunu from Niederer). Only a family-level prosody remark, p.28, quoting Downer 1961 on Mien: reduced syllables have 'weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words' -- about Mienic vowel-length languages, not Bunu/Numao. Nothing on word stress in Numao.

sources.citation: Strecker, David. 1987. The Hmong-Mien languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 10(2): 1-11.
sources.note: Nothing. Classification paper; p.3 lists '16. Pu-Nao subgroup (Bunuyu Bu-Nao fangyan).. e. Nu Mhou (Bunuyu Numao tuyu)' -- confirms identity of Numao as a Bunu (Pu-Nao) variety; no prosodic information.

sources.note: Unstopped syllables carry one of nine contrastive tones, numbered by historical category: 1 =55, 2 =35, 3 =33, 4 =11, 5 =52, 6 =42, 7 =45(4), 8 =2(3)2, plus secondary 3' =113 (from PHM aspirated/voiceless-sonorant initials); checked syllables (-p -t -k, loans) take only tones 7 [45] and 8 [11]; tone 1 open syllables end in glottal stop [55ʔ]; tones 6 and 8 breathy in careful speech; 5:6 and 4:8 hard to distinguish in rapid speech; non-final shortening 7 -> [45], 8 -> [22], 3' -> [13]; 'No tone sandhi has been discovered so far' (p.224); Meng 2001:82-83 has the same oppositions with different…

sources.note: Citation (Niederer 2002: 217, 225): contains 'a sketch of Chángpáoyáo phonology and a list of approximately three hundred words' for the Maolan dialect, with a 'distinct tonal system': p.473 reports three tone mergers reducing the eight historical categories to 5 tones (1 =33, 2 =55, 3 =13, 4 =31, 5 =52, 6 =13, 7 =55, 8 =52), no secondary split; p.510 lists presyllables /pu ta ku tɕi/. Likely also gives the Yaolu (Numao proper) tone system from the same survey (cf. Li 1983 贵州瑶麓瑶语音位系统).
